Read it in order, front to back. Every concept builds only on concepts that came before it — nothing is used before it is taught. The sign § means “section”: §7.3 is section 7.3. When an earlier idea is needed again, the text says “recall §n.n” and points back to where it was built; when a later section is mentioned early, it is named with a one-line explanation.

The book has seventeen chapters. Chapters 1–4 describe data: variables, study designs, summaries and diagrams. Chapters 5–8 build probability, sampling, estimation and the logic of the hypothesis test. Chapters 9–14 compare groups and model outcomes: parametric and non-parametric tests, correlation and confounding, linear regression, generalised linear models and survival analysis. Chapters 15–17 turn to research practice: clustered and survey data, missing data, prediction, sample size, meta-analysis and trials, then measurement and the threats to a study’s validity.

Each concept follows the same four-part structure:

  • Definition — the precise, technical statement.
  • Simplified Explanation — the same idea rebuilt from first principles, in plain language, usually with an analogy or a callback to something already covered.
  • Illustration / Example — one concrete worked example, drawn mostly from a running Community Medicine context (an under-five clinic, a CBHI household survey, a district outbreak).
  • Must-Know Notes (MD-level) — the compressed, exam- and practice-relevant takeaways.

Four further blocks appear where they earn their place:

  • Derivation — the few lines that show why a formula is true.
  • Worked Calculation — numbered steps that carry an example through to a stated result.
  • In R (optional) — the same analysis run in the free statistical software R, with its real output and a reading of what each number means.
  • Common Misreading — the tempting wrong interpretation of a result, and why it is wrong.

After each group of related concepts comes a Checkpoint, numbered within its chapter (Checkpoint 5.3 is the third in Chapter 5): a few questions to answer from memory, in your own words, before looking anything up. Trying to retrieve and explain an idea is one of the most effective ways to find out whether you understood it, and to make it stick. Answers, with the working shown, are in Appendix A at the back. Try each question before you turn there.

Conventions, cut-offs and named rules are cited author–year in the text, and the full sources are listed in the References at the end.
